newsitem.title: USA: Cordial debate sways few voters.
newsitem.headline: Cordial debate sways few voters.

text.p: Monday's headlines rated the first 1996 presidential debate civil but indecisive, and a sample of voters across the country indicated the match did little to nudge the undecided or challenge the convicted.
"Candidates Spar Widely, With Civility," said the Star Tribune of Minneapolis over its story about Sunday's night head-to-head encounter between President Clinton and challenger Bob Dole.
"Clinton Holds Ground Versus Dole," added the Chicago Tribune in its front page summary.
"It didn't change my mind," said New York stockbroker Chris Giannos. "The election is Clinton's to lose."
Giannos, a former Democrat who considers himself an independent leaning toward Clinton, said Dole "was like a boxer training for a fight. He did some nice sparring, but he didn't knock Clinton out."
Gerry Wegener, a 40-year-old network engineer from New York who also calls hmself an independent leaning toward Clinton, said the debate did little to change his views.

"Clinton won the debate. I thought Dole kind of stumbled. He didn't have much to say. I view Dole as more of an old-style politician, although he did come across as more human last night," Wegener said.

Thomas Bannon, 37, of Sharon, Mass., called the encounter "entertaining" but "I think they skirted most of the issues." Dole, he said, "Did a good job. But I think I was already set to vote for Clinton."
In Boston, 46-yeard-old George Forrest said he did not like Clinton and the matchup offered little substance for him.
"But the debate made me realize that I'll vote for Dole whereas I might have just taken a pass on the whole thing," he said.
A number of people interviewed in downtown Cleveland said the debate sharpened but did not change their views.
"I don't like Dole and it was confirmed last night. Dole's closing statement just made no sense," said Jeanne Williamson, 52, an advertising sales representative.
Phil Pasterak, 38, a Cleveland engineer, said he still planned to vote for Clinton even though he said he usually leaned Republican.

"I thought Dole was still unclear about his direction. I thought he performed badly in the debate. He did not answer the questions posed to him, and his train of logic was faulty. It had holes in it," Pasterak said.

For Marie Barton, a 68-year-old retired office manager living in Ormond Beach, Fla. who voted Republican in most recent presidential elections, the debate did little to affect her indecision about this year's choice.
"What really fries me about Dole and the Republicans is that they keep talking about people trying to scare seniors. What are we, children?" she said.

"I know how Medicare works and I like Medicare. It does a good job of covering my medical bills and no other insurer is going to do that for seniors. I don't want my benefits cut and that's that," she said.
"On the other hand I can't stand Clinton. Dole was right that he wants to take credit for everything good, but never any blame," she said.

Bob Holden, 67, a retired school teacher living in Winter Park, Fla., said he admired Dole for a long time and "there's no question he'd be a better president." But, he said, the 73-year-old Kansan "came across as just too old ...
"It's not a job for a young man but it's not necessarily a job for a man in his seventies either," said Holden, who said he planned to vote for Dole.

In Kansas City, Mo., Staci Bacca, a 26-year-old commodity broker, said the debate did nothing to sway her from voting for Ralph Nader, the consumer advocate who is running for president as the Green Party candidate.

"It was just the same old stuff over and over and over again. I didn't hear anything new," Bacca said. "I think that they're both crooks. Professional politicians that don't have any real values. Just worried about getting votes."

David Zarefsky, dean of the School of Speech at Northwestern Univklersity, said "this was probably not a debate that changed many minds. But for those only weakly committed to a candidate, it may have helped to sharpen each candidate's position and the differences between them."
The exchange "was for the most part a fair and civil discussion of the issues," he said. " Often the clash turned on who should receive credit for results that both candidates supported."
